notes.meaning: James calls his readers "brothers" because all Christians stand as equals in God's family. Jesus is the glorious Lord, and his glory is shared by every believer, rich or poor. So people who trust in him must not show favoritism. That means treating some people better just because they are rich or important.

James paints a picture of two visitors. A rich man in a gold ring and fancy clothes walks into the church meeting, and so does a poor man in dirty, worn-out clothes. The rich man is given the best seat. The poor man is told to stand or sit on the floor. Being polite to people is fine, but treating the poor as if they don't matter is wrong.
By doing this, they sort people into "better" and "worse" in their own minds. They act like judges, but their thinking is twisted. Fine clothes prove nothing about what a person is really worth.

James asks them to stop and think. God has chosen many poor people to become rich in faith and to inherit his kingdom. He does not choose only the poor. But the poor often turn to him more readily than the rich do. The people God honors, we should honor too.

Yet they had shamed the poor man. James reminds them that it was often wealthy people who bullied them and dragged them into court. They also spoke evil of the beautiful name of Christ that believers carry. It was foolish to fawn over the very people who mistreated them. James is describing what usually happened, not every rich person.

The "royal law" is the King's command to love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18). It rules over all the other laws. Your neighbor means everyone, rich and poor alike. If you truly keep this law, you are doing well.

Favoritism is not a small thing. It is sin, and God's law shows that people who do it are lawbreakers. The law even says plainly not to favor either the poor or the powerful when judging (Leviticus 19:15).

God's law is one whole, like a chain that breaks if one link snaps. Breaking one command makes you a lawbreaker, even if you keep the others. This does not mean all sins are equally bad. It means the same God gave every command, so ignoring one rejects his authority. It also shows we cannot earn our way to God by being good most of the time.

James tells them to live with the coming judgment in mind. They will be judged by "the law that gives freedom." That is the good news of Jesus, which frees us to love and obey God willingly. So their words and actions should be full of love.

Anyone who shows no mercy will be judged with no mercy. This is the other side of Jesus' words, "Blessed are the merciful" (Matthew 5:7). But mercy wins out over judgment. Our kindness does not earn God's mercy. Instead, God's mercy to us in Christ makes us merciful, and that mercy triumphs on the last day.

Now James turns to faith and deeds. Notice that he says someone "claims" to have faith. He means an empty claim, not the real thing. Can that kind of faith save? The expected answer is no. James is not arguing with Paul, who taught that we are made right with God by faith. He is correcting people who twisted that teaching into an excuse to live as they pleased.

James gives an example. A fellow believer has no warm clothes and no food. Someone says, "Go in peace, stay warm and eat well," but gives nothing. Kind words with no help do that person no good at all.
Faith works the same way. A faith that never leads to action is dead. It is not true faith, just as a corpse is not a living man. Real faith is never alone. It always bears fruit.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe "dead" here means useless, not missing. They say James is not questioning whether his readers are truly saved.

notes.meaning: Someone might say, "You have faith, and I have deeds," as if a person could have one without the other. James answers with a challenge. Faith can't be seen, so try showing me your faith without any deeds. You can't. But I can show you my faith by what I do.
Believing that God is one is good. It is the first truth of the faith. But demons believe it too, and they shudder with fear. Simply agreeing with true facts about God is not the trust that saves.
James calls the boaster "foolish," which means empty. Now he is about to give proof from the Bible. He will show that faith without deeds is worthless for salvation.

"Justified" means declared right with God, or shown to be right. Abraham had been counted right with God by faith many years earlier (Genesis 15:6). When he was ready to offer his son Isaac, that deed showed his faith was real. James is talking about the proof of faith, not the cause of being saved.

differ.view: Paul and James mean two kinds of justification. By faith Abraham was counted righteous. By the works that came after his faith, he was made righteous. James's justification is the fruit of Paul's.

notes.meaning: Abraham's faith and his actions worked together. Faith came first and led him to obey. His obedience then brought his faith to full growth, the way a seed grows into a full tree. Works did not give his faith life. They showed it was real and helped it mature.

Genesis 15:6 says Abraham believed God, and God counted it to him as righteousness. That was said long before he offered Isaac. When Abraham obeyed, those words came true in full, because everyone could see his faith was genuine. He was even called God's friend (Isaiah 41:8).

James concludes that a person is justified by deeds and not by faith alone. Here "faith alone" means the bare, lifeless faith he has been describing. Real faith always shows itself in deeds. We are counted right with God through faith, and our deeds prove that faith is alive.

differ.view: "Justified" here means shown to be righteous before people. Good works prove that faith is real, but they have no power to make anyone right with God.

Martin Luther at first struggled with this letter and called it an "epistle of straw." He did so because this teaching seemed to clash with Paul's words that we are justified by faith (Romans 3:28). Barnes reports that Luther later changed his mind and accepted it as Scripture.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think James was writing against Paul's teaching, or against a twisted version of it.

notes.meaning: Rahab was a Gentile woman with a sinful past. She believed Israel's God, and at the risk of her life she hid the Israelite spies and helped them escape another way. Her actions proved her faith was real. By naming both great Abraham and lowly Rahab, James shows that true faith bears fruit in anyone, of any people or background.

James sums it all up. A body without its spirit, or breath, is dead. In the same way, faith without deeds is dead. He does not mean that deeds give faith its life. He means that faith with no deeds is like a lifeless body, only the empty shape of faith.
